--- Strana 97 ---
Fig. 2.32 Module: First convolutional layer

--- Strana 98 ---
The number of output channels is given by the parameter num_channels,
and each kernel is assumed to be square with size kernel_size.
Internally, the module instantiates num_channels convolution PEs
(conv_pe), each responsible for computing the convolution operation for one
output channel. For each channel ch (1 ≤ch ≤num_channels), the PE is
provided with the current input feature, the corresponding weight and bias, and
control signals, and produces an output feature value (feature[ch]) along with
a done flag (flag[ch]).
After all PEs have finished their computations (i.e., all flag[ch] are set and
every PEs generates a new feature data), the module outputs the results from each
PE on output_feature[ch] and sets the ready signal (ready) to high,
indicating that valid output data is available. If only a subset of flag[ch]
signals are set, this indicates an error condition, and the module outputs an error
message and sets ready to low. If none of the PEs have finished, the outputs are
held at zero, and ready remains low.
The conv_layer2 module, as shown in Fig. 2.33, implements a parallel
multichannel convolution operation for a set of input feature maps. The inputs
include the current input feature map values
(input_feature[in_channels]), a flattened array of weights for all
convolution kernels (weight[kernel_num*in_ channels]), and bias
values for each output channel (bias[kernel_num]). The module is
synchronized by clock and reset signals (clk, n_reset), a start signal (start),
and a handshake signal from the preceding pooling layer (ready_pool) to
indicate when the input data is ready for processing.

--- Strana 99 ---
Fig. 2.33 Module: Second convolutional layer

--- Strana 100 ---
The main parameters are the number of input channels (in_channels), the
number of output channels or kernels (kernel_num), and the size of each
convolution kernel (kernel_size, assumed square).
Internally, the module instantiates kernel_num convolution processing
elements (conv_pe), each receiving its slice of the weights and the
corresponding bias. For kernel k (1 ≤k ≤kernel_num), the PE is connected to
the complete set of input channels, receives the relevant weights (weight
indexed for kernel k), and produces an output feature value (feature[k]) along
with a completion flag (flag[k]).
When all completion flags (flag[k]) are set, the module outputs the results
from all PEs on output_feature[k] and sets the ready flag (ready) to
indicate valid output data. If only a subset of completion flags are set, this
indicates an error, and the module sets ready low and displays a runtime error
message. If none of the PEs have completed, all output features are held at zero,
and ready remains low.
2.4.4 Pooling Layer Module
This part will introduce the basic element of the MaxPooling layer, the
MaxPooling processing element, and how to combine multiple MaxPooling
processing elements to build a MaxPooling layer module.
2.4.4.1 MaxPooling Processing Element
The pool_pe module, as shown in Fig. 2.34, implements a processing element
for max pooling over a fixed-size window. The main parameter is the pooling
window size (pool_size).

--- Strana 101 ---
Fig. 2.34 Module: Max pooling processing element

--- Strana 102 ---
Inputs to the module include the input value for the current window position
(input_featuremap), clock and active-low reset signals (clk, n_reset), a
start signal (start) to initiate pooling, and an enable signal (enable) to
advance the pooling operation.
Internally, the module maintains a register (max_value) that tracks the
maximum value in the current pooling window and a counter (counter) to track
the number of values processed. If reset is triggered, both registers are cleared.
During operation, if start is high and the counter equals the pooling window
size, the module resets the counter and initializes max_value to the current input
value (starting a new window). Otherwise, when enable is high, the counter is
incremented. The module compares the input value to max_value, updating it if
the new value is larger.
The combinational output logic assigns the completion flag (flag) to high
and outputs the maximum value (output_featuremap) when the pooling
window is complete (i.e., counter equals pool_size). Otherwise, the flag is
low, and the output is set to zero.
2.4.4.2 MaxPooling Layer
The pool_layer module, as shown in Fig. 2.35, implements a parallel pooling
operation over a multichannel input feature map. It receives as inputs the current
feature values from the previous layer (input_feature[num_channels]),
clock and active-low reset signals (clk, n_reset), a start signal (start) to
initiate pooling, and an enable signal (ready) indicating that input data is
available.

--- Strana 103 ---
Fig. 2.35 Module: Max pooling layer
The module parameter num_channels defines the number of channels
processed in parallel. Internally, the module instantiates num_channels pooling

--- Strana 104 ---
processing elements (pool_pe), each operating independently on its
corresponding input channel. For each channel ch (1 ≤ch ≤num_channels),
the PE receives the relevant feature map value, clock and reset, and control signals
and produces an output feature (feature[ch]) and a completion flag
(flag[ch]).
The combinational output logic monitors the completion flags. When all
flag[ch] signals are set, indicating that all pooling elements have finished
processing, the module outputs the results from all PEs on output_feature[ch] and
sets ready_pool to high to indicate valid output data. If only a subset of the
completion flags are high, this represents an error state; in this case, the module
outputs an error message, the output feature is undefined, and ready_pool is set
low. If none of the PEs have completed, all output features are held at zero, and
ready_pool remains low.
2.4.5 Activation Layer Module
This part will introduce the basic element of the ReLU6 layer, how the ReLU6
processing element works, and how to combine multiple ReLU6 processing
elements to build a ReLU6 layer module.
2.4.5.1 ReLU6 Processing Element
The Relu6_pe module, as shown in Fig. 2.36, implements the ReLU6 activation
function for a given input. The main parameter is the upper bound for the ReLU6
activation (relu6_upper_bound), which represents the value 6.0 in the
system’s fixed-point data format.

--- Strana 105 ---
Fig. 2.36 Module: ReLU6 processing element
Inputs include the value to be activated (input_featuremap), clock and
active-low reset signals (clk, n_reset), a start control signal (start), and an
enable signal (enable).
On each clock edge or failing edge of n_reset, the following logic is
executed. If reset is triggered (n_reset is low), the output
(output_featuremap) and the output flag (flag) are cleared. If the start
signal is not high, both outputs remain cleared. Otherwise, the flag is set according
to the value of enable, and the module computes the ReLU6 activation as
follows: if input_featuremap is positive and less than
relu6_upper_bound, the output is set to the input value. If the input exceeds
the upper bound, the output is saturated to relu6_upper_bound. If the input is
negative or zero, the output is set to zero.

--- Strana 106 ---
2.4.5.2 ReLU6 Layer
The Relu6_layer module, as shown in Fig. 2.37, applies the ReLU6 activation
function in parallel to each channel of an input feature map. The inputs include the
feature values for all channels (input_feature[num_channels]), clock
and active-low reset signals (clk, n_reset), a start signal (start) to initiate
activation computation, and an enable signal (ready) indicating data availability.

--- Strana 107 ---
Fig. 2.37 Module: ReLU6 layer

--- Strana 108 ---
The number of channels is specified by the parameter num_channels,
which determines how many activation processing elements (PEs) are instantiated.
Each channel has a corresponding instance of the Relu6_pe module. For each
channel ch (1 ≤ch ≤num_channels), the PE processes its respective input,
providing an activated output (feature[ch]) and a completion flag
(flag[ch]).
The combinational output logic checks all completion flags. If all flag[ch]
signals are high, indicating that all activation PEs have finished computation, the
module outputs the activated values on output_feature[ch] and asserts the
ready_activation signal. If only some flags are high, this indicates an error
condition; the module outputs an error message, sets the output to an undefined
state, and deasserts ready_activation. If none of the PEs have finished, the
outputs are held at zero, and ready_activation remains low.
2.4.6 Fully Connected Layer Module
This part will introduce the basic elements of the fully connected layer, the fully
connected processing element, and how to combine multiple fully connected
processing elements to build a fully connected layer module.
2.4.6.1 Fully Connected Processing Element
The full_pe module, as shown in Fig. 2.38, implements a single multiply-and-
accumulate (MAC) unit for a FC layer, typically used in neural network
accelerators. It receives as inputs the value of the current input neuron
(input_featuremap) and the corresponding weight (weight), both
represented in fixed-point format and clock (clk), active-low reset (n_reset),
and a start signal (start) to control operation.

--- Strana 109 ---
Fig. 2.38 Module: Fully connected processing element
On each rising edge of the clock or falling edge of n_reset, the main logic
operates as follows: if reset is active (n_reset is low), the internal multiplication
register (mul) is cleared. If the start signal is not high, mul remains zero.
Otherwise, the module computes the product of the input feature and weight and
stores it in mul.
The output (output_featuremap) is generated by truncating or rounding
the multiplication result to match the fixed-point hardware design requirements.
2.4.6.2 Fully Connected Layer
The full_layer module, as shown in Figs. 2.39 and 2.40, implements a
parallel FC layer. In each clock cycle, it receives a vector of input neurons from
the previous layer (input_feature[in_channels]) and their
corresponding weights (weight_ful1[in_channels]). The parameter
in_channels determines the number of input neurons processed in parallel.

--- Strana 110 ---
The module computes and accumulates contributions to every output neuron
(output_feature[out_neurons]) across all input batches.

--- Strana 111 ---
Fig. 2.39 Module: First fully connected layer part 1
Fig. 2.40 Module: First fully connected layer part 2

--- Strana 112 ---
For each batch, the module instantiates multiple parallel processing elements
(full_pe), each calculating the product of an input and its corresponding
weight. The outputs from these units are summed and accumulated into registers
(neuron_hidden) for each output neuron, utilizing the property of FC layers, where
input neurons contribute to every output neuron through linear superposition. The
accumulation is managed by internal counters (count, count2) that iterate over
output neurons and input batches, respectively.
The finish signal is used to reset accumulators and counters when all FC
computations for the current inference are complete. As new input data arrives
(ready is high), the counters work and accumulation proceeds. When all inputs
and outputs have been processed, the module asserts the output valid flag
(ready_ful1) and outputs the final results for all neurons as the sum of the
accumulated value and its corresponding bias.
In summary, the module’s core logic is that each group of input features is
processed in parallel; their weighted sums are accumulated into all output neurons.
Once the computation is complete, each neuron’s result is finalized by adding a
bias.
The full_layer2 module, as shown in Figs. 2.41 and 2.42, implements a
parameterized fully connected (FC) output layer, where each output neuron
accumulates weighted contributions from all input neurons. The input feature
vector (input_feature [IN_SIZE]) is first latched into registers
(hidden_neurons [IN_SIZE]). The output neurons (output_neurons
[OUT_SIZE]) each have an accumulator to sum the results over all input
neurons, and the per-neuron bias (bias[OUT_SIZE]) is loaded from file.

--- Strana 113 ---
Fig. 2.41 Module: Second fully connected layer part 1

--- Strana 114 ---
Fig. 2.42 Module: Second fully connected layer part 2
The module uses a single processing element (full_pe) to compute the
product of the current input neuron and its corresponding weight

--- Strana 115 ---
(weight_ful2), providing the result (feature1). Two counters, count_1
and count_2, are used to iterate through output neurons and input neurons,
respectively. Each time flag is high, the output neuron index (count_1_1) is
incremented, and the current product is accumulated into the corresponding output
neuron accumulator.
The sequential logic cycles through each output neuron for every input neuron,
accumulating their weighted sums. When all output neurons have been updated for
a given input, the module advances to the next input neuron. When all input and
output neurons have been processed (count_1 == OUT_SIZE && count_2
== IN_SIZE), the finish flag is set, and the final outputs are computed by
adding bias to each output neuron accumulator.
The outputs flag_ful2, count1, and count2 provide control/status for
external interfacing and weight management modules.
2.4.6.3 Classification Layer Module
The classify module, as shown in Fig. 2.43, implements the final decision
logic for a neural network classifier. It receives as input a vector of scores
(input_feature[num_classes]) for each category (e.g., ten classes for
digit recognition), along with clock (clk), input ready (ready), and active-low
reset (n_reset) signals.

--- Strana 116 ---
Fig. 2.43 Module: Classify
Internally, the module performs a maximum search to determine the index of
the class with the highest score. The combinational logic scans through all input
scores, keeping track of the maximum value found. Sequential logic then updates
the output registers on each clock edge or reset: if reset is triggered or input is not
ready, the outputs (categories, one_end) are cleared. When valid input is

--- Strana 117 ---
present (ready is high), the module sets the one_end flag and outputs the index
(categories) of the class with the maximum score.
This module is typically used at the end of the neural network computation to
convert raw class scores into a final classification result.
2.4.7 Top-Level Entity
The gdp_net module, as shown in Figs. 2.44, 2.45, and 2.46, describes the top-
level architecture of a complete pipelined neural network accelerator, structured as
a sequence of parameterizable hardware modules. The main input signals include
the global system start (start), clock (clk), active-low reset (n_reset), an
input pixel data stream (input_data), and a store flag for data buffering.

--- Strana 118 ---
Fig. 2.44 Module: Top-level entity of accelerator part 1

--- Strana 119 ---
Fig. 2.45 Module: Top-level entity of accelerator part 2

--- Strana 120 ---
Fig. 2.46 Module: Top-level entity of accelerator part 3
The inference datapath is organized as follows: pixel addresses are generated
using an address_extract module; input data is buffered and synchronized
by image_read. Two sets of kernel and bias loaders (kernel_conv1,
kernel_conv2) initialize convolutional layer weights. Each convolutional layer
(conv_layer, conv_layer2) is followed by an activation layer
(activation_layer) and a pooling layer (pool_layer), maintaining the
typical convolution-activation-pooling sequence.
The output of the second pooling layer is forwarded to a fully connected layer
(full_layer1), with weights supplied by weight_ful1. This is followed by
a nonlinearity (activation_layer_full) and a final fully connected layer
(full_layer2) with weights from weight_ful2. The final classification
result is produced by an argmax classifier (classify), which outputs the
predicted category and a one-shot end flag (one_end).

--- Strana 121 ---
Handshaking signals and ready flags ensure strict pipeline synchronization:
each module waits for input-valid flags from the previous stage before beginning
computation, enforcing a robust, data-driven hardware pipeline. All weight and
bias memories are initialized from external files, enabling flexible deployment for
various network architectures. Key structural parameters such as kernel and
pooling sizes are fully configurable.
2.4.8 Testbench Design
The testbench, as shown in Fig. 2.47, for the gdp_net module verifies system-
level functionality using a series of test images and expected category labels. The
key parameters are the image size (image_size), the total number of test cases
(num_tests), a 2D array of test images (input_image [num_tests]
[image_size* image_size]), and the expected classification result for
each image (expected_ category [num_tests]).

--- Strana 122 ---
Fig. 2.47 Module: Testbench design
For each test case, the testbench logic is as follows:

--- Strana 123 ---
1. System reset is applied by deasserting n_reset, followed by several clock
cycles to ensure all internal states are cleared. The start and store signals
are initialized appropriately.
 
2. The test image is loaded into the system pixel by pixel: each clock cycle, a
new pixel from input_image is presented on the input data line while
store is high.
 
3. Once the entire image is loaded, store is low and start is high to trigger
inference.
 
4. The testbench then waits until the one_end output from the DUT indicates
that classification is complete.
 
5. The predicted category (categories) is compared to the expected value
(expected_category) for the current test case. Pass/fail status is reported
for each case, and an error counter is incremented if any failures occur.
 
6. The process repeats for all test cases. At the end of testing, the testbench prints
a summary of the total number of tests, passes, and failures.
 
2.5 Conclusions
In this chapter, we presented a comprehensive approach to training CNNs at the
software level using TensorFlow, as well as designing a simple neural network
using System Verilog for hardware implementation. By integrating these
methodologies, we aim to provide an accessible framework for researchers and
developers to train neural networks and deploy them on FPGAs for performance
analysis. This chapter serves as a foundational resource, supporting software-
based neural network development and hardware-oriented implementation,
thereby facilitating further exploration and innovation in FPGA-based deep
learning acceleration.

3.1 Introduction
Approximate computing (AC) has become an increasingly attractive approach for enhancing
the hardware efficiency of CNN accelerators, especially in the context of embedded systems
where resource constraints are critical [1]. Among the many approximate computing
techniques, approximate multipliers (AxMs), which can trade off between the hardware
consumption and accuracy performance [2–4], have received significant attention due to the
fact that multipliers are widely utilized in the CNN hardware accelerators [5].
Because of the wide variety of available AxMs [6–8], selecting the most appropriate type
for a given CNN architecture is a fundamental step in designing an AxM-based CNN
hardware accelerator. When addressing this task, designers need to carefully consider several
key questions to ensure that approximate units are used effectively:
How can approximate components be matched to the error tolerance levels of different
CNN layers or operations?
Which exact units in the hardware design can be replaced by approximate versions
without introducing unacceptable loss in accuracy?

--- Strana 126 ---
To address these design considerations, a systematic approach is required. This chapter
introduces a structured methodology known as error matrix-based error injection (EMEI)
[9]. EMEI serves as a practical tool for designers to evaluate and deploy existing AxMs
within CNN accelerators. By using pre-characterized error rate matrices, the technique
facilitates informed decision-making when integrating approximation into processing
elements (PEs).
As a case study, the TOSAM approximate [6] multiplier is introduced and applied within
a MobileNetV2-based CNN model trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset [10] and GTSRB [11].
This example demonstrates how AxMs with varying error profiles can be strategically
assigned across different PEs, balancing efficiency and inference accuracy. Through this
case-driven approach, the chapter provides a hands-on understanding of how approximation
techniques can be systematically applied in modern CNN hardware design.

--- Strana 127 ---
3.2 Chapter Overview
In this chapter, we begin by introducing several types of approximate multipliers that are
commonly used in CNN hardware accelerators, as discussed in Sect. 3.3. Section 3.4 then
describes the EMEI method, which provides a practical means for selecting suitable
approximate multipliers with varying precision levels, while aiming to minimize hardware
overhead. Finally, Sect. 3.5 presents a set of experimental results that demonstrate the
effectiveness and practical benefits of applying the EMEI method in CNN accelerator
design. The example code is available in the GitHub repository.1
3.3 Approximate Multiplier
In the study referenced as [12], the authors introduce an innovative approach to enhancing
the efficiency of CNN hardware accelerators through the adoption of AC technologies.
Specifically, they propose the substitution of precise hardware components with approximate
hardware components. Given that convolutional layers are responsible for most of the
computational workload in CNN accelerators [13], the implementation of AxMs, instead of
precise ones, significantly reduces the hardware costs of the CNN hardware accelerator.
Emerging research in AxM technologies focuses on three methodologies: data truncation [6],
error compensation [7], and the employment of 4:2 compressors [8]. This section will
introduce works within each of these three domains.
3.3.1 Data Truncation
TOSAM AxM [6] is a type of energy-efficient, truncation, and rounding-based AxM that
supports multiple precision levels. It reduces the computational workload of the multiplier
by truncating input operands based on the position of their leading one-bit. This design
significantly enhances energy consumption and area efficiency while maintaining acceptable
accuracy levels. The methodology involves rounding input operands to the nearest odd
number, which improves total accuracy and scalability, enabling higher precision with
increased operand widths.
Compared to existing precise and approximate multipliers, the proposed TOSAM AxM
achieves superior performance in terms of delay, area, and energy consumption. This makes
it an attractive solution for error-resilient applications, including image processing,
sharpening, and classification [6].
The functionality of the TOSAM AxM is defined in Eq. 3.1. Here, (YA)t and (YB)t
denote the values obtained when A and B are truncated t bits after the first occurrence of a
“1” in their binary representation. (YA)APX and (YB)APX represent the values when A and
B are truncated h bits following the initial “1” bit, with an additional “1” appended to the
right, resulting in h + 1 bits in total. kA and kB refer to the positions of the first “1” in A and
B, respectively [6]:
(3.1)
The structure of the TOSAM AxM is depicted in Fig. 3.1. This architecture comprises
several key components:
Approximate Absolute Unit: Calculates the absolute value of the inputs.

Sign or Zero Detector Unit: Determines whether the result is zero and identifies the sign
of the result.
Leading One Detector Unit: Locates the position of the first occurrence of “1” in the
inputs.
Truncation Unit: Truncates the least significant bits of the operands.
Arithmetic Unit: Performs the primary arithmetic computation based on the truncated
inputs.
Shift Unit: Scales the result from the arithmetic unit to recover the final value.
Compatible Module: Selects the suitable accuracy level for the AxM based on input
values.

3.3.2 Error Compensation
In work [7], a low-power, high-performance AxM with configurable partial error recovery
was introduced. This design utilizes approximate adders that limit carry propagation to
neighboring bits for fast partial product accumulation. By employing configurable error
recovery, the design achieves varying levels of accuracy through the use of different
numbers of most significant bits (MSBs) for error reduction.
Additionally, this approach allows for the adjustment of the number of MSBs involved in
error recovery calculations to offer different levels of computational accuracy. The
functionality of the approximate adder is defined by Eq. 3.2, which computes one bit of the
sum result with inputs Ami and Bmi for each bit of the input operands [7]. The error
recovery signal for each adder and the total error recovery signal for the multiplier are given
by Eqs. 3.3 and 3.4, respectively.
Furthermore, an error recovery function (Eq. 3.5) adjusts the final output. In this context,

3.4 Error Matrix-Based Error Injection
3.4.1 Error Matrix of Approximate Multiplier Determination
The. working principle of TOSAM was introduced in Sect. 3.3.1. The six accuracy levels are
represented by bit retention post-truncation as (h, t). These levels are (0, 0), (0, 2), (1, 4),
(2, 6), (3, 7), and (5, 9). The error distribution matrix for each level is derived by comparing
approximate outcomes with exact values, resulting in an error ratio. This comparison is
expressed in Eq. 3.11.
In Eq. 3.11, N denotes the number of fractional bits in the binary fixed-point format. The
variables A and B represent the values obtained by directly converting the binary
representations of the multiplier and multiplicand into base-10 integers without considering
the decimal point. Ap(A, B) refers to the result of the approximate multiplication. As
evident from Eq. 3.11, the length of fractional bits does not impact the error distribution.
Therefore, for matrix calculations, both multipliers and multiplicands are treated as integers
within the range 0 to 215−1.

3.4.2 Error Injection for Determination of Suitable Approximate Multiplier’s
Accuracy Level
The utilization of error distribution matrices is essential for selecting the optimal AxM and
its precision across various conditions. A singular selection may not effectively balance
hardware efficiency with the required accuracy level. Hence, employing a combination of
AxMs with varying precision levels becomes necessary. Inspired by image processing
techniques [14], where feature maps are divided into regions of high and low significance,
we propose processing data within regions of high significance using high-precision PEs,
while data in regions of low significance are processed by low-precision PEs. Each feature
in feature maps is computed by the operations in the preceding layer, and the significance of
these features determines the precision of multipliers for their production in the earlier layer.
To select suitable AxM precision levels and arrange them effectively, the EMEI
framework includes two main steps: (1) The selection of two AxM types with high and low
accuracy levels (2) The partitioning of importance-based segments within feature maps in
CNNs
3.4.2.1 Selection of Suitable Approximate Multipliers’ Accuracy Levels
To determine the most suitable AxMs and their accuracy levels, we start by assuming that
AxMs replace all precise multipliers in CNN accelerators. This means that multiplications

--- Strana 132 ---
within convolutional, normalization, and fully connected layers will include injected error, as
specified in Eq. 3.12:
(3.12)
In this equation, M represents the error rate distribution matrix for the AxM at the
evaluated accuracy level, and M(A) refers to the data located at coordinate A within the
matrix M.
The methodology for selecting the optimal AxMs and their precision levels is as follows:
1. Order the potential AxMs in descending order of their error rates.
 
2. Begin the process of injecting error rates using matrices with the lowest error rates.
 
3. Monitor the CNN’s classification accuracy. Stop the error injection process if the
classification accuracy falls below the predefined acceptable accuracy level.
 
4. Select the current precision level of the AxM as the low-precision option for lower-
accuracy PEs in the CNN hardware accelerator. The adjacent higher-precision mode of
the AxM is selected as the high-precision option for higher-accuracy PEs in the CNN
hardware accelerator.
 
3.5 Experimental Setup and Experiment Result
To evaluate the effectiveness of EMEI, we developed two CNN models based on the
MobileNetV2 architecture. The detailed structure of these CNNs is shown in Figs. 3.5 and
3.6. For training, we utilized a subset of the CIFAR-10 dataset containing high-clarity
images, consisting of 37,074 images for the training set and 7,300 images for the testing set,
trained using the CNN shown in Fig. 3.5. Additionally, we employed the GTSRB dataset,
with 35,209 images for the training set and 12,630 images for the testing set, trained using
the CNN in Fig. 3.6 to demonstrate the performance of EMEI.

Fig. 3.6 The structure of the CNN for the GTSRB dataset
The architecture of the CNN hardware accelerator employed in our study is illustrated in
Fig. 3.7. Within this architecture, the controller module controls the operational status of
each layer’s components. Each layer includes multiple PEs, and the controller ensures
accurate memory addressing for the input and output of each PE. The input and output of
each PE are not directly sent to the memory; instead, they are stored in a buffer and then
transferred to memory through DMA. The data processed by this hardware accelerator is
represented as signed 16-bit fixed-point numbers, which include one sign bit, six integer bits,
and nine fractional bits.

Fig. 3.7 The structure of the CNN hardware accelerator
Instead of employing precise multipliers, our system utilizes TOSAM AxMs. The
selectable modes for the TOSAM AxMs are (h, t) = (0, 0), (0, 2), (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 7), and
(5, 9). Figure 3.4 presents the histogram of the error distribution matrix utilized in our
experiments. For this investigation, we set a minimum acceptable classification accuracy
threshold of 85% for the CIFAR-10 CNN and 93% for the GTSRB CNN.
3.5.1 Approximate Multiplier and Accuracy Determination
Based on the methodology described in Sect. 3.4, we injected errors into every
multiplication operation within the CNN model, following the error distribution matrix of
the AxM across various levels of accuracy, as shown in Fig. 3.4. The classification
accuracies generated from the application of different error matrices are illustrated in Figs.
3.8 and 3.9. Given that the threshold for the lowest permissible classification accuracy was
set at 85% and 93% for CIFAR-10 and GTSRB, respectively, the (h, t) mode selected for
the high-accuracy AxM was determined to be (2, 6), while the mode chosen for the low-
accuracy AxM was (1, 4). This selection was based on the observation that, at the accuracy
level (h, t) = (1, 4), the classification accuracy remained just below the threshold value.
Following the instruction in Sect. 3.4, this accuracy level was selected as the low-accuracy
multiplier, and the adjacent higher level, (h, t) = (2, 6), was chosen as the high-accuracy
multiplier.

3.6 Conclusions
In this chapter, we introduce an error injection methodology that leverages the error rate
distribution matrix of AxMs. Before detailing the methodology itself, we first review the
operational principles and structural designs of several commonly used AxMs, including
TOSAM, error compensation-based designs, and multipliers built using approximate 4:2
compressors. These foundational concepts help to establish a clear understanding of how
different AxMs function and why they are relevant for optimizing CNN hardware
accelerators.
The error injection methodology offers a structured approach for assigning suitable
precision levels of AxMs to individual PEs in a CNN accelerator. This approach enables
designers to meet the minimum classification accuracy required by the target model while
improving overall hardware efficiency through a balanced use of high- and low-precision
multipliers. The advantages of this method become particularly apparent when the hardware
cost difference between adjacent AxM precision levels is significant.
Experimental validation shows that this precision assignment strategy can maintain close
alignment between hardware-level and software-level performance, with classification
accuracy differences remaining within 3% in typical cases.

4.1 Introduction
This chapter serves as a hands-on tutorial focused on security in network-
on-chip (NoC) systems, which are widely used communication fabrics in
large-scale chips due to their scalability, lightweight design, and efficient
communication. As NoCs handle a substantial portion of on-chip
communication, they are increasingly exposed to diverse security threats.
We begin by introducing the microarchitecture and design principles of
NoC-based multiprocessor system-on-chip (MPSoC) platforms. Next, we
provide an overview of NoC-specific security issues, including
unauthorized access, data corruption, and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. A

--- Strana 142 ---
comprehensive literature review offers context on common attack vectors
and current countermeasures. We then introduce a practical implementation
of a DoS flooding attack model in the Gem5 Garnet simulator, enabling
readers to reproduce and evaluate realistic threat scenarios. Finally, we
summarize recent advances in NoC security architecture, highlighting
promising directions for future research.
To better understand the urgency of securing NoC architectures, it is
important to consider recent trends in hardware development. Machine
learning models have demonstrated remarkable performance in
classification and detection tasks, becoming vital tools in a wide range of
applications. While their application in cybersecurity has been extensively
explored, their use in hardware security remains relatively underdeveloped
[1]. Meanwhile, the demand for large-scale computing chips is rapidly
increasing to meet the needs of modern computational tasks, such as
training and inference for large language models (LLMs) [2]. Companies
like Nvidia and AMD have responded by designing high-performance data
server chips. However, the significant data throughput and computational
intensity of these workloads introduce new opportunities for adversaries to
launch sophisticated and covert attacks [3, 4]. These threats emphasize the
growing importance of developing secure hardware systems, particularly
through the use of machine learning techniques to enhance resilience
against attacks at the architectural level.

--- Strana 143 ---
4.2 Chapter Overview
This chapter begins with an introduction to the microarchitecture of
network-on-chip (NoC)-based multiprocessor system-on- chip (MPSoC)
platforms in Sect. 4.3. We describe core components such as routers and
network interfaces, common communication protocols, and typical
architectural designs. This section also introduces tools and methodologies
for modeling and simulating NoC systems, equipping readers with practical
techniques for analyzing performance and functionality—an essential
foundation for subsequent security analysis.
Section 4.4 focuses on the security challenges associated with NoCs. It
starts with a classification of common attack types, including
eavesdropping, spoofing, denial-of-service (DoS), and side-channel attacks.
Section 4.4.2 provides a step-by-step tutorial on reproducing a DoS
flooding attack using the Gem5 Garnet simulator. This hands-on guide
demonstrates how to implement and evaluate custom threat models,
offering valuable insights into real-world NoC vulnerabilities. Finally, Sect.
4.4.3 reviews current countermeasures for NoC security, highlighting their
strengths and limitations, and paving the way for future research in secure
NoC design.
4.3 Microarchitecture of Network-on-Chips
The concept of network-on-chip (NoC) as a key enabler for designing
multiprocessor system-on-chips (MPSoCs) has evolved significantly,
representing a major shift away from traditional bus-based and point-to-
point communication architectures in SoCs. Initially conceived as a scalable
solution for managing complex on-chip communication, NoCs gained
prominence with the pioneering work of William Dally, who introduced the
theoretical framework for packet-switched micro-networks. This innovation
marked a paradigm shift in the way SoC designs were conceptualized [5].
Building on this foundation, Luca Benini and Giovanni De Micheli further
emphasized NoCs as a transformative “new paradigm” for SoC design,
highlighting their critical role in addressing the communication demands of
increasingly complex and heterogeneous SoCs [6].
Figure 4.1 illustrates a typical mesh NoC architecture. In this design, the
NoC comprises nodes interconnected through links or channels. Each node,

--- Strana 144 ---
often referred to as a tile in chip design, typically includes a router, a
network interface, and various intellectual properties (IPs), such as CPUs,
caches, or specialized accelerators. Communication between nodes involves
packaging data, instructions, and information from one IP into packets,
which are then transmitted across the network. Depending on the link
width, these packets may be divided into smaller units called flits. Figure
4.1 also shows an example packet structure, derived from the Netrace
dataset [7], which demonstrates the standardized format used for efficient
packing and unpacking by routers and network interfaces based on a unified
architecture.
Fig. 4.1 A mesh-based NoC architecture
Different topologies significantly influence the structure and
performance of a NoC [8]. Topology refers to the arrangement of nodes and
channels within the network. Selecting an appropriate topology for chip
development depends on various factors, including complexity, density,
workload, and PPA (performance, power, and area). While the mesh
topology is commonly employed in MPSoCs, many other topologies exist
and can be broadly categorized as either direct or indirect. In direct
topologies, each router acts as both a source and destination for traffic, as
exemplified by ring, mesh, and torus topologies, which are prevalent in
NoCs. Conversely, indirect topologies distinguish between routers and
terminal nodes, with only the terminal nodes functioning as sources or sinks
for traffic.
The router is a critical component in a NoC, facilitating information
transfer, traffic arbitration, and control at each node. It is typically

--- Strana 145 ---
responsible for three primary functions: routing, flow control, and
switching. Consequently, its micro-architecture has a significant impact on
the NoC’s performance, particularly regarding per-hop delay and energy
consumption. A standard router microarchitecture, shown in Fig. 4.2,
includes essential components such as virtual channels (VCs), routing logic,
allocators, a crossbar switch, and buffers. VC are not required for all NoC
configurations; however, they play a crucial role in improving performance
when traffic density becomes too high for fixed, non-virtual channels to
handle. VCs enable NoCs to implement a dynamic and adaptive channel
allocation strategy [9]. This design allows the NoC to efficiently and
flexibly manage sudden spikes in high-volume traffic, ensuring smoother
communication and reduced congestion. It also contributes to mitigate
deadlock cases by cutting off the deadlock loop.
Fig. 4.2 Router microarchitecture and routing process
In operation, a neighboring router first verifies whether downstream
routers have available credits. If credits are available, the neighboring
router begins sending packets, which are written into the input buffers of
the receiving router. The receiving router then computes the routing to
determine the appropriate output port direction. Virtual channel allocation
modules manage local communication resources by dynamically assigning
VCs (buffers) to incoming packets. Following VC allocation and
arbitration, the packet undergoes switch allocation and proceeds to the
output stage via link traversal.

--- Strana 146 ---
In addition to the router, the network interface is another critical
component of NoC communication, serving as the initial point of
interaction [10]. The NI is responsible for packetizing data from the host
IPs connected to the local node and analyzing the communication
requirements specified by these host IPs [11]. Depending on whether the
packet needs to be sent via uni-casting, multi-casting, or broadcasting, the
NI adjusts certain fields within the packets to indicate the appropriate
communication mode for downstream nodes. Conversely, the NI is also
tasked with depacketizing incoming data from other nodes, converting it
into a format usable by the locally connected IPs. Due to the extensive
customization required for different applications and IP types, there is no
standard architecture diagram to represent the NI’s design.
Recent developments in NoC designs are increasingly supporting
specialized computing paradigms, particularly in machine learning as we
mentioned in the introduction. José Flich and Davide Bertozzi highlighted
the growing importance of NoCs in the era of nanoscale computing,
emphasizing that architectural decisions made today will shape the next
generation of NoCs [12]. One promising area of research is 3D network-on-
chip architectures, with Miltos Grammatikakis leading studies on the fault-
tolerant capabilities of 3D NoCs, which could revolutionize SoC design
[13]. NoC architectures are increasingly being adopted not only in
nanoscale computing but also in deep neural network (DNN) accelerators.
Traditional platforms like CPUs and GPUs face significant challenges
related to power consumption and performance when handling DNN
workloads. Beyond general-purpose processors, NoCs are more commonly
integrated into modern domain-specific accelerators (DSAs), such as DNN
accelerators, due to their superior scalability and high communication
efficiency. Chen et al. [14] proposes NoC-based DNN accelerators as an
effective solution, emphasizing their ability to reduce off-chip memory
accesses and enhance computational flexibility. By separating data
computation and communication, NoC-based designs offer improved
scalability and power efficiency (Fig. 4.3).

--- Strana 147 ---
Fig. 4.3 (a) The flattened DNN model; (b) clustering neurons; (c) mapping the clustered ANN
model to the target NoC platform
On the industrial front, several companies are actively incorporating
academic research findings into their technology stacks, transforming NoCs
from theoretical concepts into practical, real-world applications. These
advancements aim to deliver technologies that are efficient, robust, and well
suited to managing the computational complexities of modern systems.
To achieve the research objectives, a variety of modelling and
generation tools for NoC systems can be utilized, many of which have been
developed over the past decades. HORNET [15], Noxim [16], Gem5 Garnet
[17], and BookSim [18] are command-based tools, primarily developed in
C++ that provide comprehensive modelling capabilities for NoC systems.
Among these, Gem5 Garnet is particularly notable for enabling full-system
simulations, complete with a Linux OS, allowing researchers to assess
realistic performance and functionality in diverse use cases.
In addition to modelling tools, several RTL (register transfer level)
generators are available for NoCs, including ProNoC [19], RaveNoC [20],
OpenPiton [21], ESP [22], and Hermes [23]. These tools are instrumental in
rapidly implementing NoC-based SoCs or serving as design templates to
integrate IPs and customize systems according to specific requirements.
These RTL generators streamline the development process by providing
preconfigured NoC frameworks, enabling efficient hardware design and
validation. Most of these tools feature a GUI, providing users with a more
intuitive and visualized configuration experience. Additionally, they often
include early-stage simulation capabilities and brief performance
evaluations, even without requiring RTL code. Together, these tools offer a
robust suite of solutions for both simulating and building NoC-based

--- Strana 148 ---
systems, making them invaluable resources for researchers and developers
in the field.
4.4 Security in Network-on-Chips
4.4.1 Overview of Security Attacks in NoCs
NoC systems are essential for on-chip communication, making them an
attractive target for a variety of attacks. While online threats like malware
pose significant dangers, offline methods such as side-channel attacks also
compromise the integrity and confidentiality of NoC systems. Due to the
wide range and complexity of these threats, it is essential to understand
their classification. Charles et al. [24] provide a detailed taxonomy,
highlighting five primary types of attacks on NoCs: eavesdropping,
spoofing/data integrity, denial-of-service (DoS), buffer overflow/memory
extraction, and side-channel attacks.
NoC systems are vulnerable to various attacks that exploit on-chip
communication. Eavesdropping involves adversaries intercepting sensitive
data, often through hardware Trojans in routers along communication paths.
Spoofing attacks occur when malicious nodes impersonate trusted ones,
leading to data corruption, information leakage, or system collapse. DoS
attacks disrupt access by overwhelming nodes with excessive traffic, often
through flooding or tampering with packet destinations. Buffer overflow
attacks inject malicious code, causing hardware buffer overflows that
compromise shared memory in multicore systems, potentially impacting the
entire system. Lastly, side-channel attacks exploit physical variations like
power or electromagnetic signals to extract information, leveraging the high
communication density in NoC systems.
In this work, our primary focus is on DoS attacks targeting NoC
architectures. Among the various types of DoS attacks, traffic-based attacks
stand out as particularly prevalent. These attacks are especially harmful
because they compromise not only the security and integrity of NoC
systems but also lead to significant degradation in overall system
performance. This is particularly consequential in real-time and mission-
critical applications, where even minor performance disruptions can have
severe impacts. Our objective is to not only identify these attacks but also to
model them effectively, enabling the development of more robust security
solutions for NoCs. A more comprehensive discussion of DoS attacks,

--- Strana 149 ---
including their various forms and how they can be modelled within the
context of NoCs, will be provided in the following subsection.
DoS attacks, particularly flooding attacks, present significant challenges
to NoC-based systems, leading to severe performance degradation, reduced
quality of service, and increased power consumption. For instance, [25]
thoroughly examines the impact of such attacks on MPSoC performance,
identifying various attack paths, including overlaps and loop-based attacks.
Additionally, [26] provides a detailed categorization of flooding attacks,
introducing a conceptual framework that considers the number of attackers
and victims. This framework illustrates attack patterns involving malicious
IPs targeting victim IPs, offering valuable insights into how these attacks
are executed, as depicted in Fig. 4.4.
Fig. 4.4 Flooding attack simulation from Sinha et al.
Chaves et al. [27] introduced the term “Flooding DoS” to specifically
describe flooding attacks within NoC environments. This study offers a
unique perspective, highlighting that such attacks can be initiated not by
hardware Trojans but through malicious software operating on a processing
element. The research explores two FDoS implementation scenarios: one
involving an increase in the packet injection rate and the other focusing on

--- Strana 150 ---
extending the packet payload length. These findings highlight the
complexity and variety of DoS attacks, particularly flooding attacks, and
underscore the necessity for comprehensive and multilayered defense
strategies.
In this case, it developed a refined flooding DoS threat model for NoCs
by introducing an adjustable flooding injection rate. This innovation stems
from the observation that varying injection rates can produce different
impacts on NoC runtime performance and resource utilization. We
integrated this functionality into the synthetic traffic pattern benchmarks in
Gem5 Garnet, allowing users to control injection rates through newly
introduced command options.
The threat model includes two attack scenarios: (1) a single attacker
targeting a single victim and (2) two attackers simultaneously targeting a
single victim. The injected packets contain random, useless data. A key
novelty in this threat model is that normal communication across all nodes
continues without interruption, albeit at a reduced efficiency due to the
flooding attack. In this implementation, flooding traffic overlays normal
communication, degrading its performance to represent an “ideal” flooding
attack scenario, as illustrated in Fig. 4.5.

--- Strana 151 ---
Fig. 4.5 “Ideal” flooding DoS threat modelling
Additionally, this model ensures that adversaries do not compromise
network protocols or routing algorithms, maintaining the stealth of the
attack. For instance, router communication credits remain balanced because
all transactions, including those initiated by flooding attackers, are
legitimate, and malicious packets adhere to the system’s default routing
algorithm. Consequently, the NoC protocol permits the flooding attack to
persist, overwhelming the system with a surge of malicious packets without
violating protocol rules or engaging in unauthorized communications.
Consequently, system runtime characteristics, such as performance
degradation or complete system failure due to traffic congestion, vary
significantly based solely on the flooding injection rate (FIR). This
functionality was implemented within workload applications as a malicious
“Tick” function (in synthetic traffic pattern benchmark of gem5), with
adjustable input parameters for flexibility. It will be explained more in Sect.
4.4.2 by a tutorial of reproducing this threat. The right-side plot in Fig. 4.6
illustrates the relationship between latency and FIR in our flooding model.
As FIR increases, latency escalates dramatically, severely impacting system

--- Strana 152 ---
performance. For instance, latency rises from 1.1 to 60 times the normal
value as FIR increases from 0.1 to 0.9. At FIR=1, the system crashes
entirely. Lower FIR values, while more covert, still exert a sustained
negative impact on system performance.
Fig. 4.6 The increasing system latency with increasing flooding injection rate
4.4.2 Tutorial: Fine-Turning DoS Flooding Attack
Reproducing in Gem5 Garnet
4.4.2.1 Overview of Gem5 and Garnet
Gem5 is a modular, open-source, cycle-accurate computer system simulator
widely used in computer architecture research and education. It supports
multiple instruction set architectures (ISAs) such as x86, ARM, RISC-V,
and MIPS and offers various CPU models, including in-order, out-of-order,
and atomic models. Gem5 can simulate both full-system and syscall
emulation modes, making it versatile for different research needs [28].
Garnet is an on-chip network model within Gem5 that provides cycle-
accurate microarchitectural implementation of network components. It
allows detailed modeling of routers, links, and topologies, enabling

--- Strana 153 ---
researchers to study network-on-chip (NoC) behaviors and performance
[17].
We selected Gem5 with Garnet for our experiments due to its flexibility,
extensibility, and detailed modeling capabilities, which are essential for
accurately simulating and analyzing DoS attacks in NoC environments.
4.4.2.2 Setting Up the Gem5 Simulation Environment
To set up the Gem5 simulation environment with Garnet, follow these
steps:
1. Clone the Gem5 Repository:
git clone https://gem5.googlesource.com/public/gem5
cd gem5
 
2. Install Dependencies: Ensure that the necessary dependencies are
installed. This typically includes Python 3, SCons, and other libraries.  
3. Build Gem5 with Garnet Support: Use the following command to
build Gem5 with the Garnet standalone protocol:
scons build/NULL/gem5.debug
\ PROTOCOL=Garnet_standalone -j$(nproc)
This builds the Gem5 binary with the NULL ISA and Garnet
standalone protocol, suitable for network-only simulations.
 
4.4.2.3 Configuring the Hardware Architecture
Our experimental setup uses a 4×4 mesh topology with 16 nodes. Each
node is connected to a router, and the network operates with the following
parameters:
The configuration parameters listed in Table 4.1 define the structural
and functional setup of the simulated NoC environment:
Number of CPUs: The simulation includes 16 processor cores,
representing a typical multicore MPSoC platform. Each core is mapped

--- Strana 154 ---
to a corresponding node in the mesh topology.
Number of Directories: There are 16 directories used for cache
coherence. This ensures one-to-one mapping between CPU nodes and
directory nodes, simplifying coherence management.
Topology: The Mesh_XY setting specifies a 2D mesh interconnect
where routers are arranged in a grid. Communication is routed in the XY
order, meaning X-direction traversal is completed before moving in the
Y-direction.
Mesh Rows: The mesh has four rows and four columns, forming a 4×4
grid of routers. This structure ensures uniform communication distances
across the chip.
Simulation Cycles: The simulation runs for 10,000 clock cycles, which
is sufficient for observing traffic behavior and the impact of injected
attacks without incurring long simulation times.
Synthetic Traffic Pattern: The uniform_random pattern randomly
selects destination nodes for packet injection, creating a balanced load
across the network. It is commonly used for stress-testing NoC behavior.
Injection Rate: Set to 0.05, this parameter determines the probability of
packet injection per node per cycle. A moderate injection rate helps
evaluate performance under typical workloads without immediate
saturation.
Virtual Channels Per Virtual Network: Each input port supports four
virtual channels. Virtual channels are used to improve throughput, reduce
congestion, and prevent deadlock by allowing multiple logical flows over
the same physical link.

These configuration options provide a well-balanced and realistic NoC
simulation environment suitable for evaluating both performance and

4.4.2.4 Building the Hardware Architecture and Running Traffic
Pattern Tests
After configuring the hardware architecture, build the simulation
environment and run the traffic pattern tests using the command provided.
This will execute the simulation with the specified parameters, allowing
observation of network behavior under uniform random traffic.
These parameters can be set using the following command:
./build/NULL/gem5.debug
\configs/example/garnet_synth_traffic.py
--num-cpus=16
--num-dirs=16
--network=garnet
--topology=Mesh_XY
--mesh-rows=4
--sim-cycles=10000
--synthetic=uniform_random
--injectionrate=0.05
--vcs-per-vnet=4
4.4.2.5 Implementing the DoS Flooding Attack
To model the DoS flooding attack, we introduced two custom functions:
tick_attack() and flooding_pkt_gen().
The tick_attack() function builds upon the built-in tick() function
provided in the STP framework, serving as a parallel mechanism to
introduce the flooding behavior. This function is triggered on every
simulation cycle and acts as the primary controller for enabling or disabling
the malicious packet injection process via the flooding_pkt_gen() function.
The behavior is regulated by a user-defined flooding rate, which specifies
the number of malicious packets injected into the NoC per 1000 cycles.
This flooding rate is passed directly from the command line when

--- Strana 156 ---
initializing the Gem5 simulation, allowing for flexible control over the
attack intensity. Figure 4.7 presents the implementation of the tick_attack()
function, showcasing its interaction with the overall benchmark logic.
Fig. 4.7 “tick_attack()” function implementation
The flooding_pkt_gen() function performs the core tasks of generating
and injecting malicious packets. Users can configure the attack by enabling
it and specifying the attacker node(s) and victim node through command-
line inputs. Once configured, this function is invoked during each cycle,
injecting packets with the attacker node as the source ID and the victim
node as the destination ID. The injected packets, designed to be useless or
irrelevant to the regular system operations, flood the NoC at a predefined
rate. At the conclusion of the packet generation process, the
sendPkt(packet) function is called to successfully inject the customized
packets into the NoC. The implementation of the flooding_pkt_gen()
function is detailed in Fig. 4.8.

--- Strana 157 ---
Fig. 4.8 “flooding_pkt_gen” function implementation
Both functions were integrated into the file GarnetSyntheticTraffic.cc
within the Gem5 source code, ensuring their compatibility with the existing
Garnet framework. The updated file, along with instructions for its usage, is
available for public access on our GitHub repository.1
By introducing these functions, we have provided a flexible and
reusable mechanism for simulating DoS flooding attacks in NoCs, enabling
researchers to further explore and evaluate security vulnerabilities and
mitigation strategies in large-scale NoC designs.
4.4.3 Existing Countermeasures for NoC Security

--- Strana 158 ---
Extensive research has been conducted to understand the security
implications of DoS attacks in NoC systems, focusing on mechanisms for
identifying malicious activities, particularly in third-party IPs. These
security architectures typically adopt one of two design methodologies: in-
router monitoring/detection schemes and global detection frameworks. The
in-router approach involves implementing independent detection and
localization mechanisms directly within each router, allowing for localized
and real-time identification of anomalies. This method is well suited for
modular systems where individual router autonomy is essential [29, 30]. On
the other hand, global detection schemes operate by aggregating and
analyzing data from all nodes or traffic components across a defined area,
providing a comprehensive view of the system’s behavior. This collective
judgment approach enables the detection of larger, more distributed attack
patterns but often requires greater computational resources and coordination
[25, 31]. Both methodologies have their advantages and trade-offs,
underscoring the need for context-specific solutions to address the diverse
and evolving nature of DoS threats in NoC systems.
In the field of in-router security architectures, various innovative
methods have been proposed to address flooding attacks in NoC systems.
The Sniffer framework, introduced in [26], employs a lightweight
distributed machine learning model (perceptron) integrated into each router
node to accurately identify congestion caused by malicious traffic. These
perceptrons analyze multiple network parameters, including buffer waiting
time, inter-flit intervals, and virtual channel occupancy, to differentiate
between attack and non-attack scenarios. A collective decision-making
strategy further enhances accuracy by combining congestion data from
neighboring routers. Additionally, a priority mechanism ensures the smooth
traversal of probing packets during localization, minimizing disruption to
legitimate network traffic. The architecture is scalable, exhibits minimal
hardware and power overhead, and demonstrates high localization accuracy
across varied attack scenarios, including coordinated attacks with multiple
MIPs.
The AGAPE secure router architecture in [32] leverages a generative
adversarial network (GAN)-based anomaly detection framework to identify
and mitigate hardware Trojan (HT) attacks in NoC systems. The
architecture incorporates dynamic error correction hardware for fault-
injection HTs, bypass links for misrouting HTs, and channel buffers for

--- Strana 159 ---
packet-drop HTs. Using a semi-supervised GAN, AGAPE models time-
series data of various runtime NoC attributes, such as buffer utilization and
latency, to detect anomalies and classify HT types with high precision.
Instead of isolating infected routers entirely, AGAPE applies targeted
mitigation strategies, reducing performance degradation. The architecture
includes enhanced routing mechanisms, dynamic link bypassing, and state
tracking to maintain network functionality even under attack, achieving
improved detection accuracy (up to 91%) while reducing latency and power
consumption by 39% and 30%, respectively.
The secure router architecture proposed by Chaves et al. [30]. focuses
on mitigating low-and-slow denial-of-service (LSDoS) attacks in NoCs.
This architecture integrates a lightweight LSDoS monitor within the router,
positioned between the local FIFO buffer and subsequent router
components. The monitor employs a finite state machine (FSM) to detect
anomalies in packet inter-flit delays, triggering countermeasures when a
predefined threshold is exceeded. When an LSDoS attack is detected, the
monitor truncates malicious packets by injecting a tail flit, releasing
communication resources. Any remaining flits of malicious packets are
dropped, effectively neutralizing the attack. This approach ensures minimal
disruption to legitimate traffic while maintaining negligible area and
performance overheads. Experimental results demonstrate its robustness
against both single and multisource LSDoS attacks, offering an effective
solution for enhancing NoC security (Figs. 4.9, 4.10 and 4.11).

--- Strana 160 ---
Fig. 4.9 Sniffer architecture
Fig. 4.10 AGAPE router example

--- Strana 161 ---
Fig. 4.11 Router architecture with LSDoS monitor
Numerous studies have explored global detection methodologies for
addressing security threats in NoC systems, leveraging collective data
analysis for comprehensive monitoring. The secure router architecture
proposed in the study [33] introduces a lightweight and real-time
framework for detecting and localizing DoS attacks in NoC-based SoCs. It
relies on two key mechanisms: packet arrival curves (PACs) and destination
latency curves (DLCs). Each router profiles traffic during the design phase
to establish upper PAC bounds, which are used to monitor communication
behavior and flag anomalies in real time. The DLCs, recorded at each
destination IP, capture latency statistics and help identify potential
malicious sources by analyzing deviations from expected values. The
architecture integrates a leaky bucket algorithm to ensure efficient detection
with minimal overhead. Upon detecting a threat, the routers collaborate

--- Strana 162 ---
using diagnostic messages to localize the malicious IP, reducing false
positives by evaluating congestion along the network path. Experimental
results demonstrate the system’s ability to achieve timely detection and
localization with an area overhead of less than 6% and power overhead
below 4%. This framework highlights a distributed, efficient, and scalable
solution for improving NoC security against DoS attacks (Fig. 4.12).
Fig. 4.12 LSDoS Monitor
Expanding on these approaches, Atul Prasad Deb Nath and colleagues
proposed the ARK architecture in [34]. The ARK architecture introduces a
robust framework for ensuring the security resilience of NoC-based SoCs in
the presence of untrusted components. It consists of two primary
components: satellite units deployed at each router and IP, and a centralized
security policy engine (SPE). The satellite units monitor and detect critical
interface events, generate standardized frame-based packets containing
security metadata, and enforce real-time security policies by
communicating with the SPE. The SPE, acting as the “security brain,”
analyzes data received from satellite units, enforces fine-grained security
policies, and updates the system’s security state to mitigate threats such as

--- Strana 163 ---
packet misdirection, masquerading, and data tampering. This architecture is
scalable and adaptable to various attack scenarios, providing dynamic on-
the-fly detection and mitigation while incurring minimal area and power
overhead. Experimental results demonstrate its efficiency in detecting and
mitigating malicious NoC communications without significantly affecting
performance (Fig. 4.13).
Fig. 4.13 Security ARK NoC architecture

--- Strana 164 ---
4.5 Conclusions
This chapter provided a hands-on tutorial for simulating DoS attacks in
NoC systems using Gem5. Starting with an overview of NoC architecture
and security challenges, we focused on flooding-based DoS threats and
introduced a practical approach to reproducing these attacks. Readers were
guided through setting up the Gem5 simulation environment, configuring a
mesh-based NoC, and modifying traffic generation code to inject attack
packets at controlled rates. These steps enable systematic experimentation
and help assess the performance degradation caused by varying attack
intensities.
The goal of this tutorial is to equip readers with a reusable simulation
framework for studying NoC security. By integrating custom threat models
into Gem5 Garnet, users can replicate real-world vulnerabilities and
evaluate system responses. This chapter also discussed key
countermeasures from recent literature to offer broader context. We hope
this resource supports researchers and engineers in exploring, testing, and
advancing secure NoC design through accessible and replicable simulation
practices.

Network-on-Chip Security
